slo.text_verbatim: Use the approximate value 9.8m/s2 for free fall acceleration near Earth to solve problems.
slo.success_criterion: By the end you can answer a 4-mark SRQ that asks you to calculate the time or speed of a freely falling body using g = 9.8 m/s², and explain why the object's mass never appears in the working.

materials: a stone and a light ball for the drop demonstration
a coin and a small piece of paper (optional)

items.q: Equation linking vf, vi, a, t?

objectives: I can state that g ≈ 9.8 m/s² is the same for every freely falling object, whatever its mass.
I can use v = u + gt to find the time or speed of a free fall.

blocks.text: Read Section 2.5: 'If you drop a ball and a large stone from the roof of your school building, which of them will reach the bottom first?'

Stone and ball hit ground together — mass irrelevant. Galileo dropped different masses from Pisa's Leaning Tower (p.48); same landing time. Every falling object near Earth has acceleration g ≈ 9.8 m/s². Falling: +g. Thrown up: −g.

one_screen: Objective: every freely falling object near Earth has the same acceleration, g ≈ 9.8 m/s², whatever its mass. Prerequisite: acceleration a = (vf−vi)/Δt (Q: define acceleration — A: rate of change of velocity with time). Worked example: a 2 kg block dropped from rest hits the ground at 78.5 m/s; using Δt = (vf−vi)/g = (78.5−0)/9.8, Δt = 8 s — the mass is never used. Practice: (1) ball falls 5 s, find speed — v = 9.8(5) = 49 m/s; (2) stone hits ground at 39.2 m/s, find time — t = 4 s; (3) do a 5 kg and 500 g mango land together when dropped together? — yes, g is the same for both. Misconception: pupils think heavier objects fall faster; repair by asking what changes in Δt = (vf−vi)/g if the mass is 20 kg instead of 2 kg — nothing, because g has no mass term. Exit question: calculate the time for a 15 kg block dropped from rest to hit the ground at 58.8 m/s, and explain why mass does not appear in the answer — Δt = 6 s, because g is independent of mass.
